prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, enabling frequency measurement at the 1e-18 level

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B048 alone, with Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. After the full first round, the case rests on content that survived every member's scrutiny. The magic-wavelength condition removes the dominant systematic of neutral-atom spectroscopy, the trapping light shift, so that very many atoms can be interrogated at once. The concept has been realised and compared in independent laboratories at fractional uncertainties near 1e-18, which is the maturity test that matters to me as an atomic theorist, because the systematic-shift budgets (blackbody radiation, lattice hyperpolarisability, collisions) can be checked by anyone with a clock. Concrete consequences follow: the preparation for redefining the SI second, relativistic geodesy, and constraints on varying constants and dark-sector couplings. Six of eight members now prefer it as the sole part, and I note that the remaining two list it as an alternative, but I do not count that as evidence of merit. I reach the same position on scientific grounds, and I would defend it even if support were thinner. The two names map onto two different decisive contributions, the concept with the first strontium realisation and the drive to record accuracy and many-body regimes, and neither can be dropped without misrepresenting the invention.
statement.case_against: The overlap with the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize for control of single quantum systems is real and I do not dismiss it. A lattice clock needs a comb and an ultrastable laser, and ion clocks showed that optical clocks could beat microwave standards. My judgment is that the invention is nonetheless distinct, since many-atom interrogation with a trap that cancels its own perturbation is a different concept from single-ion control, and the citation must say so by naming the optical lattice clock and not optical clocks in general. Credit to Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Bloom and the Paris and PTB groups remains a genuine limitation of a two-name award that no wording fully removes, and several of my colleagues, like me, rely on recollection for the finer priority details. The redefinition of the second has not yet been adopted. I still regard that as a timing argument that does not outweigh impact already demonstrated and independently reproduced.

responses.point: Danielsson moved from B008 first to B048 as the sole part, while warning that broad opening support is not evidence of merit and may only mark a consensus safe option, and listing overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes as the main objection.
responses.response: I agree that support counts are not an argument, and I do not rely on them. My argument is that the lattice clock is a different object from a comb or a single-ion clock: the whole point is that the magic wavelength cancels the lattice light shift so that many atoms contribute, and that is what gave the statistical power and the 1e-18 reproducibility. That answers your overlap question for me, provided the citation names the optical lattice clock. I also share your wish to flag Katori-versus-Ye weighting for verification. My answer is that I would not hold the prize back for it, because both contributions are documented in the clock record, but I would not claim more precision about priority than the committee can verify.

responses.point: Kroll asked me to check the clock-comparison figures and proposed that B003 (trapped-ion quantum logic) might be a second prize part, while holding that a clean two-person prize on B048 alone is acceptable.
responses.response: On the figures: from the atomic-structure side, uncertainties at the 1e-18 level are plausible only because the blackbody-radiation shift and the higher-order lattice shifts have been characterised independently in several laboratories, and that agreement is what I would cite. I would not add specific numbers to the citation beyond the 1e-18 scale, since I am relying on recollection for the exact record values. On B003 as a second part, I do not support it. Cirac, Zoller and Blatt would bring the total to five people against the three-person limit, so the combination cannot be formed without dropping a name from B048, which I regard as an injustice to the invention, and the experimental credit in trapped-ion logic overlaps the 2012 prize.

responses.point: Mehlig sees no natural two-part pairing within three laureates and finds the two-name credit easy to defend while noting that Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and others are not captured.
responses.response: We agree that a second part would force a split of B048 that neither achievement deserves, and I now hold that position more firmly after seeing the chair's question on this. On the credit limits, I accept your point that no citation can fully protect against omitted groups. Where we differ slightly is that I would not treat that as a reason to widen the prize with a third name, because the only candidates for it have a weaker claim to the lattice-clock invention itself than the two proposed. The citation should name the lattice clock specifically and leave the broader field of optical clocks to the community.

responses.point: Pearce, now ranking B048 first, argued against adding a third name only to fill the quota and noted that the Higgs discovery (B054) remains the most consequential outstanding experimental result in particle physics, though any three ATLAS and CMS names omit others.
responses.response: I agree about not padding the credit and I accept your point on the Higgs, which I would still not place above B048 for the attribution reason I gave in round 1: three names out of two collaborations of thousands would be contested in a way Katori and Ye would not. If the committee later wants B054 it should decide whether spokespersons serve as a proxy for the collaborations, and I would also note that your declared connections to B054 and B033 are a matter for the recusal discussion if either becomes the lead. For B048 I see no conflict for you, and I think your recusal flag is irrelevant to the outcome we are converging on.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B019 (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) because a Z2 prediction was confirmed in HgTe and then in many material families, but is willing to support the clock if the committee prefers an unambiguous two-person prize, and states that she would not put it ahead on science alone.
responses.response: I take the scientific parity seriously: topological insulators have comparable independent confirmation and the prediction-to-experiment link is a real strength. I still rank B048 first because the three omitted names (Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang), the early three-dimensional work, and the 2016 prize all enter the B019 decision, and I think the committee would be forced to settle a contested priority question by fiat. That is not a statement that B019 is weaker science; it is why I keep it as my principal alternative. If your uncertainty about the 2016 overlap resolves in B019's favour and the committee were willing to honour the HgTe route explicitly, my ordering could change, but nothing in the round-1 files has done that.

responses.point: Olsson prefers B028 (Rose, Haider, Urban) as a concrete invention that removed the long-recognised spherical-aberration limit, accepts that her first-place vote is an outlier, and says B048 would be a defensible outcome.
responses.response: I accept that aberration correction is a real invention with lasting impact and that the criterion of discovery or invention rather than lifetime achievement applies to it. I appreciate your candour about the Krivanek and STEM question, which is exactly the kind of unresolved priority issue that makes a TEM-only trio difficult. The 1986 microscopy prize is a secondary consideration for me. The main difference is that B048 requires no choice between competing instrument lineages. I do not ask you to abandon your preference, but I note that we agree on the fallback and that your own statement treats B048 as defensible.

responses.point: Johansson moved from B001 to B048, citing the clean credit split and that the 2025 superconducting-circuit prize makes a near-term circuit QED award hard to justify, while flagging a possible recusal issue on B001.
responses.response: I appreciate that you separated subject familiarity from the merit argument, and I agree that B001 is not scientifically weaker, only less well timed. Your point that recognition across fields is spread by choosing B048 is secondary for me, because I would not choose a candidate for distribution reasons. What persuades me is the same independent maturity argument you accept. Since B001 is not a competitor now, I see no recusal issue arising for the outcome we are converging on.

uncertainties: Whether the citation wording (optical lattice clock, with a 1e-18-level clause) is accepted by the clock community as distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 single-ion prizes; I judge that it is, but cannot verify it from the files.
Whether credit to Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Bloom and the Paris and PTB groups is adequately addressed by a two-name award; this is a limitation that wording cannot remove.
Priority details between Katori's proposal and parallel lattice-clock work rest on recollection, as several colleagues also state, not on verified records.
Whether waiting for the formal redefinition of the second would improve the framing. I think not, but a decision by the metrology bodies to delay indefinitely would reduce my certainty about timing.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure: no specific conflict with Katori or Ye is apparent from my documented record. My field, theoretical atomic physics, is close to precision atomic measurement. I have documented collaborations with Anne L'Huillier, Ursula Keller's group, Reinhold Schuch, Marcus Dahlstrom, Luca Argenti and Paul Indelicato, none of whom is among the credited names on the shortlist. The round-1 exchange did not change this, and the chair's recusal question does not require me to step back from any shortlisted entry, including B048.
